newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- Oct jobs data key.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT MARKET OUTLOOK -- Oct jobs data key.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries hope to begin November the way October ended: with a rally. But it all depends on Friday morning's economic data -- primarily the October employment report, experts said.

The market is focusing on a consensus forecats for a 212,000 rise in nonfarm payrolls, as well as a 0.4-percent rise in average hourly earnings, all due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. Players, though, would love nothing more than to see numbers below the consensus.
"The market is telling you that it wants to do better," said a senior trader at a Japanese-owned primary dealership.

Bond prices continued to soar on Thursday. After a 3/4-point gain to 101-11/32, that brought the week's gain to 2-3/4 points. The bond's yield now stands at 6.64 percent, down 20 basis points from the beginning of the week.

"It seems to me that this market is on afterburner fumes at this point," said Steve Wood, director of financial markets research at BA Securities Inc. "But it's hard to imagine, after the run-up late in the day (Thursday), how good the (employment) number has to be to push the market up further."
Other analysts concurred in his estimate that the market may have made its big rally for the week after other economic reports.
Clearly, there's a bigger fear that the jobs data will be stronger than expected, even though the market hasn't traded that way this week, some analysts said.
"If we get strong data, we'll back off, but I don't know how much," said the trader at the primary dealer. "There are still better buyers in the market.

"There's a lot of anxiety and risk because we had a big move this week," he added. "But all the data says that the economy is slowing and the Fed won't have to move. So, as long as we have foreign central bank buyers ... then the market will do well."

In addition to the employment report, the National Association of Purchasing Management is slated to release its October index of manufacturing activity at 1000 EST/1400 GMT. The NAPM index is seen dipping to 51.0 from 51.7 in September, according to a Reuters poll. Players said that unlike most months, the NAPM report will be overshadowed by the employment report, although it will monitor the prices and supplier deliveries components. Auto sales will also be released Friday.
"It should be an interesting day," said a trader. "But employment is the most important. It should set the tone for the refunding (auctions) next week."
The market will also keep an eye on commodities prices. Thursday, the market rose, partially on the heels of nearly a four-point drop in the Knight Ridder Commodities Research Bureau (CRB) index.

"Generally, the market is feeling economic activity is slowing, which (third quarter) GDP confirmed, and inflation is in check. So, it should continue to be a favorable environment for the bond market," said David Jones, chief economist at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. "The only thing that can shake that view is sharply higher than expected payrolls, like a 250,000 to 300,000 rise. Also a 0.5-0.6 percent rise in earnings."
Analysts said that it would take a payroll gain of 150,000 or below to continue the week's rally while it's unclear how the market would react should the report be near the consensus.
Once the data are out of the way, the market will shift its focus to next week's Treasury auctions, in which more than $66 billion in bills, notes and bonds are up for sale over four days.
As a result players are wary of pushing yields too much lower for fear that the issues might not be so attractive.
